title: Spanning Continents
summary: Two railroad companies raced towards each other across America, one blasting through snowy granite mountains with thousands of Chinese workers, the other speeding across the plains. They met in Utah in 1869, where a golden spike was tapped in and the word 'DONE' flashed across the country. Canada and Russia built giant railways too, but the new tracks also brought great harm to Native American peoples and the bison.

sections.heading: Crazy Judah and the Big Four
paragraphs: Every great project needs someone stubborn enough to believe in it when others laugh. For the first railroad across the United States, that person was an engineer named Theodore Judah. Born in Connecticut in 1826, Judah had built railways in the eastern states before moving to California in 1854 to become chief engineer of the Sacramento Valley Railroad, the first railroad in California. He became obsessed with one huge idea: a line all the way across the continent. He talked about it so constantly that some people nicknamed him 'Crazy Judah'.

The great barrier was the Sierra Nevada, a wall of granite mountains rising more than 2,100 metres (7,000 feet) along California's eastern edge. Many people thought no railroad could ever cross it. Judah spent months tramping through the mountains with his instruments, measuring slopes and searching for a route. He found one: a long, steady ridge that climbed past a mining town called Dutch Flat and over Donner Pass, named after a group of pioneers who had been trapped there by snow in the terrible winter of 1846 to 1847.

Judah needed money, and he found it among a group of Sacramento shopkeepers. In 1861 they formed the Central Pacific Railroad, with Judah as chief engineer. Four of these businessmen became known as the 'Big Four': Leland Stanford, a grocer and politician who soon became Governor of California; Collis Huntington and Mark Hopkins, partners in a hardware store; and Charles Crocker, a dry-goods merchant who took charge of construction. None of them knew anything about building railroads, but they were tough, ambitious and very good at raising money. Judah then went to Washington and lobbied Congress so effectively that he helped get the Pacific Railway Act passed in 1862.

On 8 January 1863, in the pouring rain, the Central Pacific held a groundbreaking ceremony in Sacramento, with Governor Stanford shovelling the first earth. But Judah would not see his dream come true. He and the Big Four quarrelled bitterly over money and control, and in 1863 he sailed for New York, hoping to find investors to buy them out. Crossing Panama on the way, he caught yellow fever, a disease spread by mosquitoes, and he died on 2 November 1863, aged just 37. Today a mountain near Donner Pass, Mount Judah, is named after him.

The Central Pacific faced an extra problem that is hard for us to imagine. Almost everything it needed, rails, spikes, locomotives and tools, had to be made in factories in the eastern states. Because the Civil War was raging and there was no railroad across the country yet, all of it had to be shipped by sea, either all the way around the southern tip of South America or via Panama. A single locomotive could take months to arrive, and prices soared during the war. The company crawled forward. After two years it had laid only a few dozen miles of track and was approaching the steepest mountains. It also had a desperate shortage of workers, because many men in California preferred to try their luck in the gold and silver mines.

sections.heading: Into the Granite: The Chinese Workers
paragraphs: In 1865 Charles Crocker and his tough construction superintendent, James Strobridge, tried something new. They hired a crew of about 50 Chinese workers. Strobridge was doubtful at first and claimed they were too small for heavy work, but Crocker reportedly pointed out that Chinese workers had built the Great Wall of China. The new crew worked so hard and so well that the company soon hired thousands more.

Most of these men came from Guangdong province in southern China, especially from a group of country districts near the Pearl River Delta, not far from Hong Kong. Poverty, floods and civil war had made life very hard there, and news of the California Gold Rush had drawn many young men across the Pacific to a place they called Gold Mountain. By early 1867, according to researchers at Stanford University, about 90 percent of the Central Pacific's workforce was Chinese. Historians estimate that around 10,000 to 15,000 Chinese workers were on the job at the busiest times, and many more over the whole project.

They were treated unfairly. At first Chinese workers were paid about $26 a month and had to buy and cook their own food, while white workers received meals as well as higher wages. In June 1867 around 3,000 Chinese workers went on strike, only days after an explosion killed several workers, demanding $40 a month, a ten-hour working day and shorter shifts in the dangerous tunnels. The company cut off their food supplies, and after about eight days the strike ended, but the workers had shown they were not powerless, and pay rose over time. Many Chinese workers brought their own cooks and ate a varied diet of rice, dried fish, vegetables and tea. Because they boiled water for tea, they may have suffered less from illnesses carried by dirty water.

Their work was astonishing. To cross the Sierra, the Central Pacific had to drill a string of tunnels through solid granite, several of them packed close together near Donner Summit. The longest, the Summit Tunnel, was about 1,660 feet (around 500 metres) long. Workers attacked the rock with hand drills, hammers and black powder, and at first they could advance less than about 30 cm (one foot) a day at each rock face. To speed up, the engineers cut a vertical shaft down into the middle of the mountain so crews could dig outward from the centre as well as inward from both ends, giving four rock faces at once. They also began using nitroglycerin, a powerful but dangerously unstable liquid explosive, mixed on site by Chinese workers. Progress rose to more than 1.5 feet a day, but accidents with explosives killed workers.

The winters were brutal. In the winter of 1866 to 1867, storm after storm dumped huge amounts of snow on the mountains. Workers lived and worked in tunnels dug through the snow drifts, and avalanches swept away camps and men. To protect the finished line, the company later built about 37 miles of wooden snow sheds, long roofed tunnels of timber that kept snow off the track. Crews finally broke through the Summit Tunnel in 1867, and by June 1868 passenger trains were running through it.

Nobody knows how many Chinese workers died building the Central Pacific, because the company did not keep records of their deaths. Estimates range widely, from dozens to well over a thousand. What is certain is that the line over the Sierra Nevada could not have been built without them, and for over a century their part in the story was often left out.

sections.heading: Across the Plains: The Union Pacific
paragraphs: Meanwhile, far to the east, the Union Pacific was getting started. It held a groundbreaking ceremony in Omaha, Nebraska, on the west bank of the Missouri River, in December 1863, but serious construction did not begin until July 1865, after the Civil War had ended.

The man running the company was Thomas C. Durant, a clever and ruthless financier who cared more about money than about trains. He hired Grenville Dodge, a Union general and experienced railway surveyor, as chief engineer. Dodge chose much of the route across Nebraska and Wyoming and over the Rocky Mountains, and he once discovered a key pass through the Laramie Mountains while being chased by a war party, or so he later claimed. The actual track-laying was led by two brothers, Jack and Dan Casement, who ran their crews almost like an army.

And in a way it was an army. Many of the Union Pacific's workers were veterans who had just come home from the Civil War, from both the Union and the Confederate sides. Thousands more were Irish immigrants, many of whom had fled the terrible Irish famine of the 1840s. There were also freed African Americans, German and other European immigrants, and, in Utah, Mormon workers hired under contracts.

Laying track across the open plains became an amazing routine. A work train carried the crews, with bunk cars, dining cars and a blacksmith's shop, and it moved forward as the track grew. Wagons brought up wooden ties, which were set in place on the graded earth. Then teams of men grabbed iron rails weighing hundreds of kilograms, ran forward and dropped them into position, while others came behind to fix them and hammer in the spikes, about three blows to a spike and hundreds of spikes to every mile. On good days the Union Pacific laid several miles of track. In 1867 it built about 270 miles, and in 1868 almost 360.

As the railhead crept west, temporary towns sprang up wherever the workers camped, full of tents, saloons and gambling halls. People called them 'Hell on Wheels', because they were rough, lawless places, and when the track moved on, many of them were simply packed onto trains and set up again further west. A few, like Cheyenne in Wyoming, survived and grew into real cities.

There was also something rotten at the top. Durant and other Union Pacific leaders set up a construction company called Crédit Mobilier of America and then paid it hugely inflated prices to build the railroad, pocketing the profits while the railroad itself sank into debt. They also handed out shares to members of Congress. When the scheme was exposed in 1872, it became one of the biggest political scandals of the century.

sections.heading: Ten Miles in a Day and a Golden Spike
paragraphs: By 1868 the Central Pacific had finally burst out of the mountains into the flat deserts of Nevada, and now both companies raced. Each was paid by the mile, so every mile mattered. For a while the two sets of graders even passed each other in Utah, building parallel embankments side by side, until Congress stepped in and chose a meeting place: Promontory Summit, north of the Great Salt Lake in Utah Territory.

Charles Crocker of the Central Pacific was so confident in his crews that he reportedly bet Thomas Durant $10,000 that they could lay ten miles of track in a single day, something nobody had ever done. On 28 April 1869 they tried. The materials were carefully lined up in advance. Chinese workers raced ahead setting ties, and a team of eight Irish rail handlers lifted and placed the rails, about 1,000 tons of iron between them. By evening they had laid just over 10 miles (about 16 km) of track, a record that has never been broken by hand. A sign was later put up beside the line to mark the spot.

Then came 10 May 1869. At Promontory Summit, two locomotives rolled up nose to nose: the Central Pacific's Jupiter, a wood-burner with a big funnel chimney, and the Union Pacific's No. 119, a coal-burner. Railway officials, workers, soldiers and a few onlookers crowded round. A last tie of polished California laurel wood was laid, and several ceremonial spikes were tapped into pre-drilled holes, including the famous golden spike, made of 17.6-carat gold and weighing about 14 troy ounces (about 430 grams). It had been the idea of a San Francisco businessman named David Hewes.

A telegraph wire had been connected so that the whole nation could 'hear' the final blows as clicks on telegraph sounders. Leland Stanford raised a silver-headed maul, swung at the final spike and, according to many accounts, missed. The telegraph operator sent the signal anyway. Then a one-word message flashed down the wires to both coasts: 'DONE'. In cities across the country, crowds celebrated with cannon salutes, bells and parades.

Here is an important detail. The golden spike is NOT still in the track. It was pulled out right after the ceremony, to stop it from being stolen, and replaced with an ordinary iron spike. The golden spike was later given to Stanford University, and today it is displayed at the university's Cantor Arts Center in California. A famous photograph by Andrew J. Russell shows the two engines and a crowd of men shaking hands and holding up bottles. Very few Chinese workers appear in it, even though a Chinese crew had laid the final rail on the Central Pacific side. In 2019, at the 150th anniversary, descendants of Chinese railroad workers gathered at Promontory to restage the photograph and make sure their ancestors were remembered.
The site is now the Golden Spike National Historical Park, where working replicas of the Jupiter and No. 119 steam towards each other on summer days.

sections.heading: A Continent Shrinks
paragraphs: Before 1869, a journey from the east coast to California could take around six months by wagon, or weeks by ship and land via Panama. After the railroad opened, the trip from New York to San Francisco took about a week. By 1876 a special express train, the Transcontinental Express, did it in a record 83 hours and 39 minutes, less than four days. The whole line from the Missouri River at Omaha and Council Bluffs to Sacramento was about 1,900 miles (about 3,000 km), and a short extra line soon linked Sacramento to the shores of San Francisco Bay.

Freight became far cheaper too. Experts estimate that the railroad moved goods across the country for something like a tenth of the cost of wagons. Californian fruit, wine and wheat could travel east, while factory goods, books and machines flowed west. Mail that once went by stagecoach or Pony Express now went by train. Towns grew up all along the route, and the government's land grants were sold to settlers who poured onto the plains, often lured by railroad advertising.

The railroads also made enormous fortunes, sometimes unfairly. Leland Stanford became one of the richest men in America, and after his only son died young, he and his wife Jane founded Stanford University in his memory. Meanwhile the Crédit Mobilier scandal showed how close railroad money had come to politics. The government loans to the two companies were eventually paid back with interest by 1899.

Most of the Chinese workers who had built the Central Pacific went on to other jobs. Some went home to China, while others farmed, built levees, mined, or worked on dozens of other railroads in the American West and in Canada. Yet in 1882, the United States passed the Chinese Exclusion Act, which banned almost all new Chinese workers from coming to the country. The people who had helped join the nation together were being shut out of it.

sections.heading: The Cost for Native American Nations
paragraphs: The railroad crossed the homelands of many Native American nations, including the Lakota, Cheyenne, Arapaho, Pawnee, Shoshone and others. To them it was not an empty wilderness waiting to be crossed, but home: hunting grounds, sacred places and the lands of their ancestors. The 'free' land the government handed to the railroads had been taken from them, often in ways that broke treaties the United States itself had signed.

Some nations fought back against the survey parties and construction crews, and the US Army was sent to protect the line, with generals such as William T. Sherman and Philip Sheridan directing the campaigns. The railroad then allowed soldiers, weapons and supplies to move quickly onto the plains, which made it much harder for Native nations to resist. Settlers followed the tracks, fencing land, ploughing grassland and building towns.

The deepest wound was the destruction of the bison, also called buffalo. At least 25 million bison once roamed North America, and some estimates are far higher. For nations of the Great Plains, bison provided almost everything: meat, hides for clothing and tipis, bones for tools, and a central place in religion and culture. The railroads helped to wipe them out. Railroad lines across Kansas and Colorado split the animals into a northern and a southern herd. Railroad companies hired hunters to feed their workers. Some passengers even shot at bison from train windows for fun.

Worst of all, trains made it easy to ship bison hides east, where factories turned them into leather, including belts for driving machines. In the winter of 1872 to 1873 alone, more than 1.5 million bison hides were loaded onto trains. Professional hunters slaughtered the animals by the hundreds of thousands. Some army officers openly said that killing the bison would force Native nations onto reservations, and in 1874 President Ulysses S. Grant declined to sign a bill that would have protected the herds. By the late 1880s, only a few hundred bison survived in the United States, and fewer than a hundred lived in the wild.

For the Plains nations, the loss was a catastrophe. Without the bison, many families went hungry and were forced to depend on government rations on reservations. A Crow leader named Plenty Coups later described it this way: when the buffalo went away, 'the hearts of my people fell to the ground'. Today, thanks to conservation efforts and many Native nations working to restore herds, bison have come back from the brink, but the story reminds us that one group's great achievement can be another's great loss.

sections.heading: Canada's Ribbon of Steel
paragraphs: North of the border, Canada faced a similar challenge. In 1871 the colony of British Columbia, on the Pacific coast, agreed to join the new country of Canada, but only on one condition: a railway must be built to connect it with the east. It was a gigantic promise for a country of only a few million people. The line would have to cross the rocky, lake-filled wilderness north of Lake Superior, the vast prairies, and several ranges of mountains, including the Rockies and the Selkirks.

The project started badly. In 1873 Prime Minister John A. Macdonald's government was caught in the 'Pacific Scandal', in which railway promoters had given large sums of money to his party, and the government fell. Some government-built sections were started in the 1870s, but the work only really took off after the Canadian Pacific Railway company was formed in 1881. An energetic American manager named William Cornelius Van Horne was hired the next year and drove the work forward at an incredible pace.

Through British Columbia, the hardest and most dangerous work was done by about 17,000 Chinese workers, many recruited from China and many from California. They were paid less than white workers, given the riskiest jobs such as blasting tunnels on cliffs above the Fraser River, and many fell ill in harsh camps. Historians estimate that hundreds of them died, perhaps 600 to 800, though exact numbers are unknown. When the line was nearly done, Canada imposed a 'head tax' on new Chinese immigrants to discourage them from coming.

On 7 November 1885, at a place called Craigellachie in the mountains of British Columbia, a company director named Donald Smith drove the last spike, a plain iron one. A famous photograph shows him bending with his hammer as a crowd of men in hats looks on. The first passenger train left Montreal on 28 June 1886 and reached Port Moody, near Vancouver, on 4 July. The railway helped hold Canada together, but on the prairies it also helped push aside the Métis and First Nations peoples, much as in the United States.

sections.heading: Across Siberia, and a Puzzle About Time
paragraphs: The greatest railway of all was built in Russia. Russia stretched from Europe all the way to the Pacific Ocean, but Siberia, the huge eastern part, had almost no roads that wheeled vehicles could use. Its rivers mostly flowed north into the frozen Arctic Ocean, not east to west. To defend its Pacific coast, to move troops and settlers, and to trade with China, the Russian government decided to build a railway across the whole of Siberia.

Construction was announced in March 1891, and in May that year the heir to the throne, the future Tsar Nicholas II, helped start the work at Vladivostok on the Pacific coast. Work then went forward in sections at the same time, from both ends and in the middle. At times tens of thousands of workers laboured on the line, including soldiers and convicts, through scorching summers, swarms of mosquitoes and winters that could fall below minus 40 degrees.

The biggest obstacle was Lake Baikal, the deepest lake in the world, surrounded by steep cliffs. At first, trains were carried across the lake on giant icebreaking ferries, the Baikal and the Angara, which took about four hours to cross. The Angara survives today as a museum ship in the city of Irkutsk. In winter, when the ice became too thick even for icebreakers, passengers and goods crossed the frozen lake on sleighs, and according to accounts from 1904 the Russians even laid temporary rails across the ice for a short time. A railway around the southern end of the lake, the Circum-Baikal line, with dozens of tunnels, was finally completed in 1904.

To save time, Russia also built a shortcut through Manchuria in China, the Chinese Eastern Railway. But after Russia lost a war with Japan in 1904 to 1905, it wanted a route entirely on its own soil. That last section, along the Amur River, was finished in 1916, completing the Trans-Siberian Railway as we know it. Between 1906 and 1914 alone, the railway carried around four million peasant settlers east to new farms in Siberia.

Today the main Trans-Siberian route runs about 9,289 km (5,772 miles) from Moscow to Vladivostok, the longest railway line in the world. A through train takes about a week and the line spans eight time zones, so passengers keep changing their watches as they go.

But the long lines also created an odd new problem. When the transcontinental railroad opened, every town along the way still set its clocks by the Sun. When the Sun was highest in the sky, it was noon. Because the Earth turns, noon arrives a little later as you travel west, about four minutes later for every degree of longitude. So Omaha's noon was not Sacramento's noon, and the clocks of Chicago, Salt Lake City and every little station in between all disagreed. Imagine trying to write a timetable for a train crossing a whole continent when every station keeps its own time.

So here is the puzzle. If a train leaves one town at 12 noon, what time is it when it pulls into the next town? Nobody could agree, and with fast trains sharing the same tracks, that confusion could be dangerous. The answer, it turned out, would be invented not by astronomers or kings, but by the railways themselves.

deepDive: Historians today tell the transcontinental story very differently from the triumphant version of 1869. One big shift concerns the Chinese workers. For about a century, official histories and celebrations largely ignored them; the famous Promontory photograph barely includes them. Since the 2010s, the Chinese Railroad Workers in North America Project at Stanford University has gathered archaeological finds from work camps, company payroll records and family histories, because almost no letters or diaries written by the workers themselves survive. Its researchers estimate that 10,000 to 15,000 Chinese workers were employed at peak, making up roughly 90 percent of the Central Pacific's workforce by 1867, but they stress that the number who died is genuinely unknown: the company recorded no deaths, and newspaper reports from 1870 about bones shipped home to China contradict each other, with figures ranging from about 50 to 1,200. That is why careful writers avoid giving a single death toll. Wages are also debated, because sources compare different things (monthly versus daily pay, with or without food). What is clear is that Chinese workers usually cost the company noticeably less than white workers. A second debate concerns money and efficiency. Because the government paid the companies by the mile, with triple payments in mountains, both sides had reasons to build fast and sometimes poorly, and stretches had to be rebuilt soon afterwards. The Crédit Mobilier scandal showed how insiders could profit from construction while the railroad itself carried the debt. Economic historians such as Richard White have argued that the transcontinentals were built before there was enough traffic to justify them, and that their political influence did lasting harm; others reply that they knitted the nation together and repaid their federal loans by 1899. Finally, historians of the American West now treat the destruction of the bison as a central part of the railroad story. Rail lines split the herds, carried hunters in and hides out (more than 1.5 million in the winter of 1872 to 1873 alone), and let the army move quickly, so the loss of the bison and of Native lands cannot be separated from the engineering triumph.
funFact: The famous golden spike was only in the track for a few minutes: it was pulled out straight after the 1869 ceremony and is now on display at Stanford University's Cantor Arts Center.
